title: A Wedding and a Final Battle
overview: Heaven celebrates God's judgment on the corrupt city called Babylon and announces the Lamb's wedding, and then a rider from heaven, whom Christians identify as Jesus, defeats the beast and its armies.

parts.label: Heaven celebrates Babylon's fall (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The woman condemned here is the city called Babylon from chapters 17 and 18, pictured as a prostitute who led the world astray. Most scholars think John meant Rome, and many also see in her any power set against God. A vast crowd and the figures around God's throne shout 'Hallelujah' (Hebrew for 'praise the LORD') because God has judged her for killing his servants, and the smoke rising forever means her ruin is final.

parts.label: The wedding of the Lamb (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: In Revelation 'the Lamb' is Jesus, and his bride is God's faithful people, a clean contrast to the corrupt woman of chapter 17. Her bright linen is both 'given' to her and called the 'righteous acts' of God's people (v. 8), and Christians have long debated whether the weight falls on God's gift or on the faithful lives of his people.

parts.label: The invitation and the angel (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: An angel announces a blessing on everyone invited to the Lamb's wedding feast. When John falls down to worship him, the angel stops him because he is only a fellow servant and worship belongs to God alone. The last line is worded differently in different translations, but it seems to mean that true prophecy, at heart, points to Jesus.

parts.label: The rider from heaven (vv. 11-13)
parts.note: Nearly all readers take this rider, called Faithful and True and 'the Word of God,' to be Jesus, with fiery eyes that see through everything and many crowns showing his rule over all. His robe is already bloodied before any battle (translations differ between 'dipped' and 'sprinkled'), and because the image echoes Isaiah 63, some read it as his enemies' blood, while many others see his own blood shed on the cross.

parts.label: His army and weapon (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Heaven's armies wear the same white linen as the bride and simply follow him, and they are never shown fighting. His only weapon is a sword coming from his mouth, which most readers take as his word, and the line about ruling the nations with iron (from Psalm 2), the winepress of God's anger (from Isaiah 63) and the title 'King of kings' all say he holds final authority to judge.

parts.label: A grim feast and defeat (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: An angel calls the birds to a 'great supper of God,' a grim mirror of the Lamb's wedding feast borrowed from Ezekiel 39, and the text plainly says kings, soldiers and ordinary people, free and slave, die and their bodies are eaten. No fight is actually described: the beast and the false prophet (the oppressive power and its deceiving spokesman from chapter 13) are seized and thrown alive into a lake of fire, and the rest fall to the sword from the rider's mouth.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the rider's victory (vv. 11-21) describes a future, visible return of Jesus to end history, a symbolic picture of how his word overcomes evil in every age, or an image tied mainly to the fall of the Roman Empire in John's own day.
think: When people who have suffered under a cruel power celebrate its fall, what makes that feel like justice to you, and what would make it feel like something else?
